title: Where authority comes from
hookLine: Protestants say scripture alone is the final authority; Catholics and Orthodox read scripture within the church's living tradition

cards: Paul and Silas slip out of one Greek city by night and arrive in a town called Berea. Paul speaks in the synagogue. The listeners don't simply nod along, and they don't throw him out either.
They open the scriptures and keep checking, day after day, whether what he said holds up. Acts admires them for it: "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica."
Which raises a question that would one day divide churches: when a teacher and a text seem to disagree, who has the final word? Today's word: sola scriptura.

teach.b: Sola scriptura is Latin for scripture alone, a watchword of the Protestant Reformation. Luther and other Reformers said the Bible is the final authority, over every teacher, council and pope.

Tradition can be good and useful, they said, but scripture is the judge of it. And they pointed to Berea, where people "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so," even with an apostle in the room.
Catholics and Orthodox Christians see it another way. For them, scripture and the church's living tradition belong together.
The New Testament was written inside the church, and the whole Bible was read aloud in its worship and handed on with its teaching, so it is read within that tradition, not apart from it.
Catholics speak of the church's teaching office guarding the faith; the Orthodox, of the councils, the early fathers and the mind of the church.
They point to Paul: "stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle." By word, or by letter. Both.
Each side has its reply. Protestants say the apostles' teaching is now found in their writings, so scripture is where you check it.
Catholics and Orthodox ask who decides what scripture means when sincere readers disagree.
Protestants add that scripture alone was never meant to be scripture with no history: Lutheran and Anglican churches, among others, still say the old creeds, holding that they agree with the Bible.
Underneath is a question from ordinary life too: when good voices disagree, whose do you trust, and why?

how: Protestant churches teach that scripture is the final authority, often while still saying the ancient creeds; Catholic and Orthodox churches read scripture together with the church's tradition, councils and teachers.

o: scripture alone as the final authority
the Bible read silently, alone, at home
scripture read only in its first languages

games.q: who said what about authority — tap the pairs.
p: hold the traditions, by word or epistle

s: sola scriptura means ignoring all history and creeds
Lutheran and Anglican churches, among others, still say the old creeds, holding that they agree with the Bible.
Catholics and Orthodox read scripture within the church's tradition
for them, scripture and tradition belong together, handed on in the church.
Acts criticizes the Bereans for doubting Paul
Acts admires them: "these were more noble than those in Thessalonica."

games.q: you're in the synagogue at Berea, and a traveling teacher named Paul has just said something new about the scriptures. what do you do?
o: accept every word, since he's clearly sincere.
go home and search the scriptures, day after day.
drive him out of town before he causes trouble.
games.why: the Bereans "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so," and Acts calls them noble for it. Protestants and Catholics alike can admire that care, and still read it differently.

practice: Bring to mind one question that matters to you, and notice where you go first for an answer: a book, a pastor, a parent, a friend, your own gut.

Then ask, gently and without grading it, why that voice: because it has been right before, because it loves you, or because it was simply there first? If you pray, you can bring the question to God as well.

wordCard.voice: Sola scriptura. Latin for scripture alone: the Protestant teaching that the Bible is the final authority over every other voice.

orig.note: Latin: scripture alone, a watchword of the Reformation.

carryVoice: Your line: where do you stand? It's an old question, and an honest one. See you tomorrow.
